context.heading: Like a mare among chariots
context.body: He compares her to a susah ("mare") among Pharaoh's chariots. Egyptian chariots were pulled by stallions, so a mare among them would draw every eye; others think the image is simply a prized, richly decorated royal horse. Either way, it is high praise for striking beauty and poise.

context.heading: Perfume from far away
context.body: Her nerd ("nard") was a costly perfume oil from the Himalayan region, carried west on long trade routes. Myrrh and henna (vv. 13–14) were luxuries too. Mary of Bethany later poured a pound of nard on Jesus (John 12:3). The Song uses rare fragrance to say that love is lavish.

context.heading: Who is speaking?
context.body: The Song has no narrator, so readers follow the speakers by the Hebrew's masculine and feminine forms, which English hides. Many translations add headings like "She" and "He" to help. Notice how much of the Song is the woman's voice: she speaks first and most often.

theology.title: Desire made by God
theology.body: Genesis 2 ends with the man and woman naked and unashamed, and the Song returns to that garden joy. God made bodies, attraction and marriage and called them very good (Genesis 1:31). Scripture neither worships desire nor despises it; it places it inside covenant love.

theology.title: A song read two ways
theology.body: Jewish teachers read the Song at Passover as God's love for Israel, and many Christians, from early church writers to Spurgeon, have read it as Christ and His church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Others stress the plain sense: married love between a man and a woman. Many hold both, letting human love point beyond itself.

application.title: Dark, yet lovely
application.body: She knows people stare at her sun-darkened skin, yet she calls herself lovely (vv. 5–6). She neither hides nor boasts; she simply refuses to let critics name her.
application.question: How would you describe your own body if you used the words of God and the people who love you instead of your harshest critics?

application.title: The neglected vineyard
application.body: She kept everyone else's vineyards and let her own go untended (v. 6). Many people pour themselves into work and other people's demands while their own soul or marriage quietly grows weeds.
application.question: Which vineyard of your own have you neglected while tending everyone else's?

context.heading: A wildflower, not a garden rose
context.body: She calls herself a chavatstselet ("crocus" or wildflower) of Sharon, the coastal plain, and a lily of the valleys. These were common wild blooms, not prized garden roses. She is being modest, and he answers that among other women she is a lily among thorns (v. 2).

context.heading: Little foxes in the vines
context.body: A shual ("fox" or jackal) was known for raiding vineyards just when the grapes were young and tender. The couple asks for help catching them before the harvest is ruined. Many readers see a picture of small problems that quietly damage a growing relationship.

theology.title: Belonging that runs both ways
theology.body: "My beloved is mine and I am his" (v. 16) echoes the language of God's covenant: "I will be their God, and they will be My people" (Jeremiah 31:33). Mutual belonging is how God describes His own commitment. Human marriage, at its best, mirrors that faithfulness.

theology.title: Resting in His shade
theology.body: She sits in the shade of the apple tree and enjoys its fruit (v. 3). Scripture often pictures God as shade and shelter (Psalm 121:5). Christians who read the Song of Christ and the church have long found here the soul's delight in resting in Him, though the first meaning is human love.

theology.title: Winter is past
theology.body: The spring poem (vv. 10–13) pictures new life after a cold, barren season. Scripture uses the same hope for God's renewal of His people (Isaiah 35:1–2). The God who designed seasons also brings seasons of joy after long waiting.

application.title: Not before its time
application.body: The charge in verse 7 assumes desire is strong enough to need guarding. Waiting is not a denial of love but a way of respecting it.
application.question: Where are you rushing something that would be better if you let it come in its time?

application.title: Catch the small foxes
application.body: Relationships rarely collapse from one blow. They erode through small, unaddressed habits: a dismissive tone, a phone at dinner, a resentment left unspoken.
application.question: What small fox is getting into your closest relationship right now?

context.heading: A carriage fit for a king
context.body: The mittah ("bed" or couch) here is a portable litter carried on poles, a status symbol for royalty. Sixty warriors with swords guard it against "the terrors of the night" (v. 8). Travelers and wedding parties were tempting targets for bandits, so the escort is both pageantry and protection.

context.heading: Her mother's house
context.body: She brings him to her mother's house, to the room of the one who conceived her (v. 4). In Israel a young woman lived with her family until marriage, and mothers often helped arrange the match. The detail roots her love in family and public commitment, not secrecy.

theology.title: Coming up from the wilderness
theology.body: "Who is this coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke?" (v. 6). The wording recalls Israel's journey through the desert, led by pillars of cloud and fire. Many interpreters hear an echo of God bringing His people up to the land, as a groom brings home his bride (Jeremiah 2:2).

theology.title: The Bridegroom's joy
theology.body: Solomon's wedding is "the day of his heart's rejoicing" (v. 11). Scripture describes God the same way: "as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you" (Isaiah 62:5). Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20).

application.title: Seeking in the night
application.body: Her search happens at night, when absence feels largest. Longing is not proof that something is wrong with you; it shows what you love.
application.question: What do your restless nights reveal about what you are really longing for?

application.title: Make it public
application.body: This wedding happened in the open, with crowds, family and a crown. Commitment grows strong when it is spoken before others instead of kept vague.
application.question: What commitment in your life needs to move from private intention to public promise?

context.heading: My sister, my bride
context.body: Achot ("sister") was a common term of affection in ancient love poetry, including Egyptian love songs. It does not mean a blood relative. It adds the security of family belonging to romance: she is both his chosen bride and as close to him as kin.

context.heading: An orchard called paradise
context.body: Pardes ("park" or orchard) is a loanword, probably from Persian, for an enclosed royal garden. Through Greek it became our word "paradise." Some scholars take it as a sign of later editing; others note that trade words traveled early. Either way, she is pictured as a garden like Eden.

context.heading: Come down from Lebanon
context.body: He calls her from Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon, the high northern peaks where lions and leopards roamed (v. 8). The wild mountains picture distance and danger. Leaving them to come to him is a picture of trust: love draws her into safety with him.

theology.title: Seen without flaw
theology.body: "There is no flaw in you" (v. 7) is the language of love, not a medical report. Paul uses the same picture: Christ gave Himself for the church to present her "without stain or wrinkle" (Ephesians 5:27). What the groom sees in love, Christ makes true by grace.

theology.title: A garden for one
theology.body: The locked garden (v. 12) pictures faithful, exclusive love. God's covenant with His people has the same exclusiveness: "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Exodus 20:3). Faithfulness is not a cage but the wall that lets a garden flourish.

application.title: Say it specifically
application.body: He does not assume she knows he loves her; he names specific things he delights in. Specific praise lands in ways general compliments never do.
application.question: Who in your life needs to hear specific words of delight from you this week?

application.title: Guard the garden
application.body: A garden without a wall is soon trampled. Exclusive commitment needs practical fences: what you watch, whom you text late at night, what you share with whom.
application.question: Which wall around your marriage, or your future marriage, needs repair right now?

context.heading: Asleep, yet awake
context.body: "I sleep, but my lev ("heart") is awake." In Hebrew the heart is the center of thought and will, not just feeling. She is half asleep and restless, which is why many read the scene as a dream. It explains the strange, shifting quality of what follows.

context.heading: My soul went out
context.body: Literally, "my nephesh ("soul") went out" at his leaving. The phrase describes the whole person failing, a sinking sense of loss. When she finally opens, he is gone, and her small delay turns into a desperate search through the city.

context.heading: Watchmen on the walls
context.body: City watchmen guarded walls at night and treated a woman alone in the streets with suspicion. Here they strike her and take her cloak (v. 7). The scene is painful and brief; it shows how much she risks to find him, and how harsh the world feels without him.

theology.title: The feast of love
theology.body: The voice in verse 1 that says "Eat, friends, and drink" is unnamed; some think it is the wedding guests, others God Himself. Either way, the blessing is clear: married love is a feast, not a guilty secret. Scripture's story ends with a wedding feast too (Revelation 19:9).

theology.title: Altogether lovely
theology.body: Her praise ends, "He is altogether lovely" (v. 16). Christians who read the Song of Christ have long sung these words about Jesus, whose beauty is His character, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). Read plainly, it shows love that delights in the whole person.

application.title: Opened too late
application.body: She hesitated over small comforts, her robe and her washed feet (v. 3), and missed the moment. Delayed responses usually cost more than we expect.
application.question: What invitation, from God or from someone you love, are you postponing for the sake of comfort?

application.title: Know why you love
application.body: When asked what makes him special, she has an answer ready. Love that cannot say why it loves soon grows thin.
application.question: If someone asked what makes Jesus, or the person you love, worth it, what specific answer would you give?

context.heading: Who is the Shulammite?
context.body: This is the only place she is named, as Shulammit (v. 13). It may mean a woman from Shunem, or a feminine form of Solomon's name, something like "Solomoness," the perfect match for her king. Both names share the sound of shalom ("peace").

context.heading: Tirzah and Jerusalem
context.body: He compares her to Tirzah and Jerusalem (v. 4). Tirzah, whose name sounds like "pleasing," was the northern kingdom's capital before Samaria (1 Kings 16:23–24). Pairing the two great cities is like calling her the beauty of the whole land.

theology.title: Love found again
theology.body: In chapter 5 he disappeared; now she knows exactly where he is (v. 2). Separation in the Song gives way to reunion. Scripture's whole story moves the same way, from Eden lost to a city where God dwells with His people (Revelation 21:3).

theology.title: One among many
theology.body: Royal courts held many women (v. 8), yet he says "my dove, my perfect one, is unique" (v. 9). Solomon's own many wives turned his heart away (1 Kings 11:3–4), but the Song holds up the ideal of Genesis 2:24: one man and one woman, joined for life.

application.title: Overwhelmed again
application.body: He asks her to turn her eyes away because they overwhelm him (v. 5). Long familiarity tends to dull our wonder at the people we see every day.
application.question: When did you last really look at someone close to you and let yourself be amazed?

application.title: Comparison that celebrates
application.body: Queens and concubines praise her too (v. 9). Comparison usually breeds envy, but here it becomes celebration.
application.question: Whose good qualities could you celebrate this week instead of measuring yourself against them?

context.heading: A prince's daughter
context.body: He calls her "daughter of a nadiv ("noble")." She may not be royal by birth; her bearing makes her one. The praise moves upward from her feet, likely as she dances, and each image borrows from Israel's own landscape.

context.heading: Pools, towers and mountains
context.body: Heshbon, east of the Jordan, was known for its reservoirs, and Mount Carmel rises over the sea in the north (vv. 4–5). Damascus and Lebanon mark the far north. Describing the beloved through places gives the poem its sense of a whole land in bloom.

theology.title: Desire set right
theology.body: After the fall God told the woman, "Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you" (Genesis 3:16). In verse 10 the same rare word returns, but now his desire is for her, with no ruling. The Song shows love healed of the fall's strain, a taste of what redemption restores.

theology.title: Gifts held with thanks
theology.body: Wine, fruit, spring flowers and delights "new as well as old" fill this chapter (v. 13). Every good gift comes from the Father of lights (James 1:17). The Song invites gratitude, not guilt, for pleasures God designed and placed inside marriage.

application.title: Out to the fields
application.body: She invites him away from routine to the countryside (vv. 11–12). Couples who never step out of the daily grind slowly become managers of a household rather than companions.
application.question: When will you next step away from routine simply to enjoy the person you love?

application.title: New as well as old
application.body: She has saved up delights both new and old for him (v. 13). Love keeps both the familiar and the fresh.
application.question: What new way of showing love could you offer someone who has only known your old ways?

context.heading: Jealous as the grave
context.body: Qinah ("jealousy") here is not petty suspicion but fierce, protective commitment, the kind God claims when He calls Himself jealous (Exodus 34:14). Paired with Sheol, the grave that never gives back, it means love holds on as stubbornly as death itself.

context.heading: My own vineyard
context.body: Solomon owned a vineyard at Baal-hamon and leased it to tenants for a thousand silver pieces (v. 11). She answers that her kerem ("vineyard"), herself, is hers to give. All of Solomon's wealth cannot buy what she freely gives to one man.

context.heading: Affection in public
context.body: In her culture a woman could kiss a brother in public but not a man she was courting (v. 1). She wishes she could show her love openly without scorn. Custom shaped how love was expressed, and the Song respects that while longing for freedom.

theology.title: Many waters cannot quench it
theology.body: In Scripture "many waters" often picture chaos and threat (Psalm 93:4). Love that survives the flood points beyond romance to God's own love, which neither death nor anything in creation can overcome (Romans 8:38–39). Jesus proved it by going through death itself.

theology.title: Love cannot be bought
theology.body: Verse 7 says anyone offering all his wealth for love would be scorned. Grace works the same way: God's love is a gift, not a purchase (Isaiah 55:1; Ephesians 2:8–9). The Song ends with a beloved who is invited, not owned.

application.title: Guard the younger ones
application.body: Brothers plan to protect their little sister until she is ready (vv. 8–9): a wall gets silver towers, a door gets cedar boards. Love includes protecting those not yet ready for adult choices.
application.question: Who younger in your life needs your protection more than your opinion right now?

application.title: Not for sale
application.body: Advertising sells romance as something you earn with looks, money or the right moves. The Song says real love is given, never purchased.
application.question: Where are you trying to earn or buy a love that can only be received?
